extracted.intended_audience: law students, scholars, and patent practitioners interested in smartphone patent litigation and Apple v. Samsung
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and practical standards used in assessing and litigating smartphone-related patents (utility and design), drawn from interviews and case-history analysis of Apple v. Samsung. Focuses on claim drafting, patent quality, damages, jurisdictional strategy, and standard-essential/FRAND issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims and specification clarity / readability
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should be described the technology in a correct and concise way; it should be readable by a lay person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting claims and specification clearly is really important for jury trials; the interviewee noted Apple's claims are easy to read while Samsung's are difficult regardless of technical level. Ease of reading helps juries and affects litigation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents: trade-offs (limits vs advantages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents allow for actions involving a low risk and high reward, but this depends on a balance between the limits and the advantages of the design patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents do not have the same protections as a utility patent in scope or term, but are much less expensive to file and take less time before issuance. They are commonly used to protect ornamental design and GUIs (e.g., D618,677, D604,305).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages under 35 U.S.C. §289: whole-product vs apportioned recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Under article 289 of US patent law, the amount of damages can be calculated based on the infringer's total profit (the entire product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a debate whether damages should be based on the whole product or on a percentage apportioned to the infringing portion. In technology-intensive devices with many patents per product, awarding total profit risks overcompensation and could hinder innovation; interviewees expressed concern about this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability and USPTO reexamination: prior art/anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be rejected or tentatively invalidated based on prior art or being anticipated/unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: USPTO tentatively invalidated several of Apple's utility patents and issued first office actions citing prior art; Patent ’915 claims were rejected as anticipated or unpatentable. Ex parte examinations and office actions matter materially to litigation posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-essential patents and FRAND/licensing complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard-essential patents (SEPs) are patents required to comply with an industry standard and raise special licensing issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEPs (e.g., 3GPP/UMTS patents) create difficult patent-licensing problems because many different patent holders cover different parts of a product. FRAND obligations and SEP status affect enforcement strategy and damages/licensing negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business model influence on litigation posture
rubrics_metrics.description: A company's business model (e.g., 'innovation' company vs 'manufacturer') affects its approach to patents and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple (innovation/software/GUI focus) was reluctant to license and protected designs aggressively; Samsung (manufacturer/hardware focus) initially emphasized quantity of patents. These business-model differences shape decisions to file suits, defend, or license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional/legal-system differences affecting case strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between national legal systems (e.g., U.S. vs South Korea) change litigation dynamics and strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States uses juries and the same court hears validity and infringement, while South Korea has a bifurcated system (Patent Court handles invalidation; district courts handle infringement). Foreign defendants may face translation and procedural disadvantages in U.S. courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury instructions and verdict complexity / jury comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury instructions and verdict forms in patent trials can be extremely complex and difficult for lay jurors to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees cited 100-page verdicts and verdict forms with hundreds of discrete questions (e.g., 700 points across 84 instructions). The scientific/technical knowledge of jurors and the burden placed on lay juries is a significant factor in trial fairness and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and market-selection strategy for filing suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting forums/venues in major markets familiar to the plaintiff (e.g., U.S.) is a strategic choice in patent enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple leveraged familiarity with the U.S. legal environment and in-house counsel; plaintiffs often choose jurisdictions that maximize favorable procedures and potential remedies. Outcomes varied across UK, Germany, Korea and the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of litigation on corporate IP organization and patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile litigation can drive companies to reorganize IP functions and improve patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samsung responded to litigation by forming an in-house patent department and later focusing on improving patent quality and creating a patent development group; litigation produced both costs and strategic gains (market recognition/brand benefits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent subject matter for GUIs and ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents can (and were in the Apple cases) used to claim ornamental designs and graphical user interfaces (e.g., D604,305 covers a GUI for a display screen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patent claims focus on 'ornamental design' and have been used to pursue 'look and feel' claims against competing smartphones; diagrams/figures are central to design patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals, invalidation, and judicial standards (e.g., 'article of manufacture')
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate decisions and evolving judicial standards (such as the Supreme Court’s standard for 'article of manufacture') materially change infringement/damages outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Apple–Samsung litigation saw USPTO invalidations, Federal Circuit reversals, en banc reinstatements, and Supreme Court involvement on the 'article of manufacture' question—demonstrating that evolving legal standards and appeals can overturn jury awards and alter damages calculations.
